# Types Without a Checker {#sec-types}

The desire is not for a particular compiler. It is for the situation in
which a name admits only the values that mean that name, in a shape you
can rely on, with the structural work done by the runtime's garbage
collector instead of by a borrow checker. Rust, Zod, Pydantic, an S3
constructor ritual, and an S7 property are the same mental model at
different distances from the bits. R's gap is that *defining* the type is
not a pleasant, first-class act. You assemble it.

That gap is not a reason to lower the standard. If the work is production
work, invalid states are unrepresentable. "Mostly conventions" is how you
describe a prototype, not a package other people call.

## The ritual you have already been performing

The S3 version of parse-don't-validate is a small protocol, repeated until
it becomes muscle:

- `new_*` builds the structure and does not check
- `validate_*` states the laws and fails with a classed error
- the user-facing constructor calls both, and is the only door
- `as_*` coerces at the boundary and then goes through the door
- `format_*` / `print` / `str` make the value legible

That *is* "illegal states unrepresentable." It is unrepresentable by
convention, which means a later edit can build the object through `new_*`
and skip `validate_*`, and the type system will not notice. The protocol
works in the packages where someone is strict about the doors. It drifts
in the packages where the doors multiply.

S7's contribution is not a new philosophy. It is a place to put the
protocol so the drift has to work harder:

- property contracts live on the property
- joint laws live on the class validator
- the constructor is the door
- generics are a stronger dispatch story when the verbs and the nouns
  both grow

Its cost is authoring. Next to a Zod schema or a Pydantic model, an S7
class is verbose, and the official examples often stop at `class_any`
plus a check inside a method. That teaches the syntax. It does not teach
the reason you reached for a class. The
[S7 design notes](https://docs.jimbrig.com/s7-design-notes/) are the
attempt to write the missing practice down: what knowledge the model
carries, where a rule lives, when a property should itself be a class,
how editable values differ from snapshots and from reference owners. This
chapter will not repeat that book. It will connect it to the metal, and
to the envy.

## The envy is a diagnostic

Zod and Pydantic make parsing the default gesture. You write the shape
once. Construction fails or you hold a value. Consumers trust the type.
The authoring experience is the feature. People adopt the library because
the schema is shorter than the bugs it prevents, not because they read an
essay about bounds.

S7 can express the same designs. A property can name a class, a union, a
base type, a validator, a getter, a setter. A class validator can state
laws that mention more than one property. `convert` can sit at the edge
where JSON becomes a domain value. The machinery is further along than
the examples suggest. What is missing is the worn path: the way a
competent author reaches for a reusable property the way a TypeScript
author reaches for `z.number().int().min(0).max(255)`. Until that path
exists, production S7 will keep looking under-typed, not because the
objects cannot carry the law, but because `class_any` is the path of
least resistance and the checks leak back into the methods.

The metal already ratted this out. In the notebook, a property defined as
`p = class_any` inspects as an `S7_property` record. The names visible in
the dump include `name`, `class`, `getter`, `setter`, and `validator`.
The record's length is 6; the paste elides one name, so this book will
not invent it. The getter, setter, and validator slots in that particular
property are Nil. `class` points at the empty `S7_any` vector. The
structure for a real property contract is allocated. The example left it
blank and postponed the law to whoever uses `p` later.

That is the whole complaint, photographed. Filling those slots is the
work. A scalar-or-null string is a type, expressed as a union or as a
property validator, not as `class_any` followed by `if (!is.null(x))` in
every method. An enum of five statuses is a class or a property whose
validator knows the five strings, not a `character` and a prayer. A color
with channels in `0:255` stores the channels under validators and exposes
brightness as a getter, so brightness cannot drift out of agreement with
the channels. An API response becomes one class per reusable object, with
coercion at the edge and nowhere else.

| The law | Where it lives |
| --- | --- |
| This field's shape, range, and presence | the property |
| These fields together | the class validator |
| Wire format into the domain | the constructor, or `convert`, at the boundary |
| What we do when we talk to the world | verbs on a handle, or generics on the values |

Checks inside methods rediscover the law at every call site. They do not
compose. A property validator composes: every constructor, every
replacement, every subclass that reuses the property, gets the same door.

## S3 when you already own the ritual

Use the manual protocol when the vocabulary is small, the type is a thin
wrapper, and you already trust yourself to keep the doors closed. Use it
when the community already speaks the class (`data.frame`, an httr2
response) and a formal property model would be a translation nobody
asked for. Use S7 when you are inventing the model: schemas, configs,
enums, validated quantities, anything that will grow a second property
and a third invariant. Use neither as a costume. An S7 class full of
`class_any` is a list with a longer error message. An S3 class with no
constructor is a string someone set an attribute on.

The dispatch difference is real and secondary. S7's generics are a better
instrument when verbs and nouns multiply. They do not fix a model that
was never written. Choose S7 when you want the contracts attached to the
object *and* you are willing to fill in the slots the dump already showed
you. Choose S3 when the ritual is short enough to see in one screen and
you will actually perform it.

## Print methods are part of the type

Hadley's packages are the existence proof that this is not academic. A
finished type has a `format` that tells the truth in one line, a `print`
that uses it, and a `str` that does not dump the SEXP. That is not
decoration on top of an object system. It is how a value announces itself
in the REPL, which is still where R is used, including by the person who
wrote the package and has forgotten the shape. @sec-appearance pushes
this further, toward views as a separate contract. For this chapter it is
enough to say that a constructor without a format method is half a type.

Functional composition is the other half of the same craft. Small verbs,
each accepting a defended value and returning one, compose. A class
hierarchy that you have to enter to get anything done does not compose
with the pipe, the script, or the test. The OO in a good R package is the
minimum that makes the verbs generic and the values meaningful. The rest
is functions. That is a taste. It is also what the language is good at,
once you stop apologizing for the missing checker and supply the parse
yourself.

## Where to spend the verbosity

Verbose types and boring call sites means the bet paid off. Verbose call
sites mean the rules were left in the methods. Move a constraint into a
property until constructing the object feels as dull as calling
`integer()`. Dull is the goal. The interesting thinking happens once,
when you decide what the name admits, and then it stops happening in
every function that receives one.

Do not spend the verbosity on temporary lists inside a function. A local
`list(a = 1, b = 2)` does not need a class. Spend it at boundaries: the
wire, the file, the public argument, the value you put in a package's
return position. Those are the places other code will otherwise
rediscover the law, badly, under time pressure.

The companion book works the design consequences in detail: property
versus class, presence versus default, snapshots versus reference owners,
the checking ladder, dispatch as a vocabulary of verbs. Start at the
[overview](https://docs.jimbrig.com/s7-design-notes/00-overview.html) if
you want that argument at full length. The claim this chapter adds is
only that the runtime is not the obstacle. The authoring path is. The
nodes will happily carry a strict model. Someone has to write the model
as if the slots were the point, because they are.
